title: Indian Students Are Ditching the American Dream. Europe Is Rolling Out the Red Carpet.
excerpt: A new DHS rule capping student visas at four years, rising U.S. costs, and a landmark EU-India mobility deal are reshaping where India's 626,000 annual study-abroad aspirants choose to go.
body:
• India's overseas student outflow dropped to 626,000 in 2025 from over 908,000 in 2023, as tighter visa rules and rising costs deterred applicants from the U.S., U.K., and Australia.
  • The DHS formally published a rule on July 16 capping F-1 visa stays at four years and cutting the post-graduation grace period from 60 to 30 days, effective September 15.
  • European tuition is 50% to 80% cheaper than the U.S., and the EU-India trade deal signed in January includes structured mobility pathways for students and workers.

A. Shrinikheathan, a 22-year-old engineering graduate from Chennai, had every reason to follow his family's well-worn path to an American university. Instead, he is learning German and applying to master's programmes in Germany, drawn by tuition that costs a fraction of a comparable U.S. degree and industry links that lead directly to jobs.

"The world is becoming more multi-polar. Earlier, the U.S. was all that everyone was talking about," Shrinikheathan told Reuters, calling American and Canadian education "wildly more expensive."

He is far from alone. India's total overseas student outflow plummeted to roughly 626,000 last year from a peak of more than 908,000 in 2023, according to Indian government data, a decline driven by tougher visa regimes, spiraling costs, and a weakening rupee that makes every dollar of foreign tuition hurt more.

Washington Tightens the Screws

The latest blow landed on July 16, when the U.S. Department of Homeland Security formally published a rule abolishing the decades-old "duration of status" framework for international students. Under the old system, F-1 visa holders could remain in the country as long as they were enrolled in a programme and followed the rules, with no hard expiration date on their immigration paperwork.

The new regulation imposes a strict four-year cap. Students needing more time must petition the federal government directly for an extension or leave and re-enter under a new authorization. Universities, which previously had the power to extend stays on their own, have been stripped of that authority.

The rule also slashes the post-graduation grace period from 60 to 30 days, leaving graduates half the time to apply for another visa category, find employment, or arrange departure. It takes effect on September 15, though it faces congressional review.

"As and when there are issues of difficulties brought to our attention in regard to genuine travellers and students, we take up those issues with the US side so as to minimise the difficulties that our people face."

— Randhir Jaiswal, MEA Spokesperson

India's Ministry of External Affairs has acknowledged the anxiety. Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said at a press briefing last week that while visa rules are a sovereign matter, New Delhi is in active contact with Washington to advocate for Indian students caught in the transition.

Europe Steps Into the Vacuum

As American doors narrow, Europe is opening wider. The EU-India trade deal signed in January 2026 includes a dedicated mobility framework offering easier visa pathways, clearer post-study work routes, and mutual recognition of Indian qualifications, the first time a major economic bloc has built structured channels for Indian talent at this scale.

"For the first time, a major economic bloc is saying, 'We want Indian talent at scale.'"

— Arnav Kumar, Co-founder, Leap

The economics are stark. European tuition fees run 50% to 80% lower than their American equivalents, according to education consultant KC Overseas, with living costs further widening the gap. For families already stung by a rupee that has steadily lost ground against the dollar, the math increasingly favors Berlin over Boston.

Early enrollment data bears this out. Indian enrollment in the Netherlands climbed to about 3,700 in 2025-26 from 2,630 in 2018-19, making Indians the third-largest non-EU student group there, according to Statistics Netherlands. Eindhoven University of Technology reported roughly 2,140 pre-enrollments from India for the coming academic year, up from about 1,390 the previous year. Leiden University's Indian intake for regular master's programmes jumped to 120 this year from 70 in 2021.

Education consultancy Europe Study Centre said inquiries have jumped 25% to 30% since the trade deal. "Europe is the red-hot destination" for families put off by rising costs and tougher visa rules elsewhere, said director Sivaraman Pandian.

Arnav Kumar, co-founder of study-abroad platform Leap, projects a 60% to 70% jump in Indian student and worker flows to Europe over three to five years. "Indian students have been growing in Europe without any overarching framework. Now, we have structured pathways from education to employment," he said.

Challenges Remain

The European pivot is not without friction. Students cite language barriers, housing shortages in cities like Amsterdam, intense competition for local jobs, and the need for specialized skills that match host-country industries. Some have also flagged concerns about the rise of far-right political movements and hardening attitudes toward foreigners in parts of the continent.

"If somebody says you will get a job in this country, don't blindly believe it. Just because you studied in that country, it does not entitle you to get a job," cautioned Pandian. "You study, and you develop a skill-set; your doors are open."

What Comes Next

Whether Europe's courtship translates into a durable shift depends on how smoothly the EU-India mobility deal is implemented. India and the EU have committed to working over five years on social security pacts with individual member states and are setting up a tech-focused office to guide students and professionals through the process.

For now, the direction of travel is clear. Consultants say Indian students are increasingly matching destinations to career goals: Germany for engineering, the Netherlands for work-life balance, Portugal for affordable postgraduate research, and France for management.

Chennai-based engineer T. Suthir, who is exploring colleges in the Czech Republic and Italy, summed up the changing mood: "Earlier, before the deal was finalised, my family was saying Europe is not good. Now, they are saying it's good."
